text: Hello, it’s Grete. Today’s chapter starts with paper dolls and a little girl who hates her new shoes. It ends with a secret told after dark. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 4, and collect two new cards about real people. Today’s question: why was this the moment Annemarie’s parents had to tell her the truth?

All week you’ve been noticing small signs: soldiers on a corner, a king who rode alone, a lock on a shop door. Today, add up the clues. One small sign might be nothing. Four signs pointing the same way are a pattern. Ask what all of them, together, are telling you.

The sentence to fix is about real history, and it’s full of names that need capitals: the name of a group, the name of a people, and the name of a country. Look back at the model to see how a sentence begins and ends.
Today is review, and some answers are already correct. In grammar and spelling, tap only the mistakes. If you tap one that is fine, it costs you. So read each one twice before you decide.

This is the last night of stars. Four words climb the handle of the Little Dipper, and the last one leads you to the North Star. The two roots you know are here again, plus one new word about water. Read the meaning, find the root.
Last match of the week. See if you can do it with no misses at all. Then try one more thing: say all four words in one sentence about Chapter 4. It’s harder than it sounds.

This little draft about Chapter 4 has some apostrophes that don’t belong. Owner-words like hers, its and theirs never take one. But a name, like Lise’s or her sister’s, does. Tap only the sentences with a real problem.

Some of these words are spelled correctly, and some have lost their hidden letter. For each one, say the related word, the one where the quiet part gets loud. If the letters don’t match what you hear, tap it.

Today’s Courage Watch is about being trusted. Annemarie’s parents decide she is old enough to hear the truth, and that means she is old enough to be brave with it. When I was ten, my father told me something I had to keep to myself. I remember feeling frightened, and proud at the same time.

The first part of this chapter is light, almost funny. Enjoy it, and ask yourself why the author put it here. Then notice the room getting quiet once Kirsti is asleep. Listen to how carefully the grown-ups choose their words, and notice what changes for Ellen tonight.

Now you write. The questions ask what Annemarie learns tonight, what one careful word really means, and how her life is different by the end of the chapter. Then you’ll find proof in the book for each of the reasons you wrote last time.

For the second question, look for the word the grown-ups use for what the Nazis plan to do. Then explain what Annemarie understands it really means. The difference between the polite word and the truth is the whole point.

Your reasons say why you believe your claim. Today, you prove them. For each reason, find one moment in Chapters 1 to 4, and write where it happens. A strong piece of evidence is specific: something a character does or says that anyone could find in the book.

I didn’t go to the synagogue. My family went to church on Sundays. But my friend Ruth did, and I remember the morning before the New Year, when she came to our door with her mother, both of them very quiet. They didn’t stay long. Years later I understood: they were passing on the warning, door to door, the way the rabbi had asked.

This is Rabbi Marcus Melchior. On the morning before the Jewish New Year in 1943, he stood in front of a full synagogue and told everyone the Nazis were coming in two days. Don’t stay at home, he said. Tell everyone you know. Because people listened, and passed it on, most Danish Jews were warned in time.

Georg Duckwitz was a German. He worked for the very government that planned the raid. When he learned the date, he could have stayed silent. Instead he secretly told Danish leaders, and the warning spread. Years later, Israel honored him as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, a title for people who risked themselves to save Jews.
Aqueduct. A stone channel that leads water to a town.
Deduce. To lead your thinking to an answer, like a detective.
Induce. To lead someone into doing something.
Disrupt. To break apart. Last word, and the North Star shines.
